name: Closed vs open posture

card.summary: Closed versus open posture is the body-language contrast between hunched, folded positions and expanded, upright ones, which people adjust to look more confident and approachable.

quick.overview:
An open posture means uncrossed arms and legs, an upright chest and expanded stance; a closed posture is slumped, folded or contracted. People use the open version to appear more confident and approachable, which is part of how they come across physically.

Research is mixed. The 2010 power-posing study reported hormonal and behavioural effects, but later replications confirmed little beyond felt power.[1] Experiments on open posture have found small effects on memory and on detecting lies.[2][3]
quick.how: Practitioners describe sitting or standing with arms uncrossed, shoulders back and chest open, and leaning toward the other person. Nurse-training models such as SOLER and SURETY teach open posture for communication.[4]
quick.risks: Posture changes are not medically risky. Forcing an unnatural posture can be uncomfortable, and effects on behaviour or hormones have not been reliably shown.

lead: Closed versus open posture describes two contrasting ways of holding the body. Open posture, with uncrossed limbs, an expanded chest and upright spine, is associated with confidence, while closed or slumped posture is read as defensive or low-power. People work on it to change how they look and are perceived.

The idea was popularised by the 2010 power-posing study by Carney, Cuddy and Yap, which reported that expansive poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol; Cuddy's 2012 TED talk spread it widely.[1] A 2015 replication found effects on felt power but not on hormones or behaviour, and Carney later said the evidence was undeniable against the original claims.[1]

Other work has examined open versus slumped postures directly. One pair of experiments found open posture slowed emotional judgments and helped recognition of positive words.[2] Another found open posture improved detection of naturalistic lies.[3] In a real job-selection assessment, men more often sat in closed postures and women in open ones.[5]

angle.text: Open posture changes how a person's frame reads to others. Practitioners use it to look more confident and relaxed.

paras: Open posture is expansive and upright with arms and legs uncrossed; closed posture is contractive, with crossed arms or a slumped trunk. Studies often contrast the two without a neutral baseline, and critics call this a source of confusion in power-posing research.[1]

The 2010 Psychological Science study with 42 participants started the popular claim, and Cuddy's 2012 TED talk made it famous.[1] Egan's SOLER model, introduced in 1975, recommends open posture in nurse education, and a later critique proposed the SURETY alternative.[4]

After the 2015 failure to replicate hormonal effects, a 2017 special issue found no effect on power-related behaviour, and a 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, none on physiology, and uncertain behavioural effects.[1] An open-posture experiment found better lie detection, particularly for more empathic judges.[3] Another found open posture slowed emotional judgments.[2]

Laboratory studies have tested open and closed postures on memory, judgment and deception detection.[2][3] A randomised trial protocol on corrective exercise for upper crossed syndrome has been registered, which concerns postural alignment rather than perception.

timeline.event: Egan introduces SOLER, recommending open posture.[4]
Carney, Cuddy and Yap publish the power-pose study.[1]
Ranehill et al. fail to replicate hormonal effects.[1]
